\chapter{The Field and the Farm --- Field, Farm, Livestock, Harvest, Shepherd}
\label{ch:la-granja}
\hlchaptermodality{299}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the field, the farm, the livestock, the harvest and the shepherd in Spanish, and say I am from the country.}

Complete ES-C299-pastor: name all five of a holding in order, and say what three of them were named after.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el campo]{el campo — flat ground, and everything pitched on it}

\label{lesson:ES-C299-campo}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what is inside \emph{dubitare}? (\emph{Duo}, two.) And what does \emph{ni hablar} refuse? (The conversation, not just the request.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pueblo — what usually sits in the middle of it.
  \item el valle — the shape of the land it lies in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CAM-po}, stress on the first part. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is hard. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el campo} — \textquotedblleft{}the field,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the countryside,\textquotedblright{} everything that is not the town.

Latin \textbf{campus} meant flat open ground — not a farmer's field particularly, just level land with nothing on it. Which is precisely why so much got pitched there.

An army stopped on flat ground, so a \textbf{camp} is one. A season of fighting was spent out on it, so a \textbf{campaign} is one. Whoever fought for a village in single combat was its \emph{campio}, the man of the field, which is English \textbf{champion}. And when American colleges wanted a word for their grounds, they took \textbf{campus} back whole and unchanged.

So the same flat ground gave English a tent, a war, a hero and a university. And it gave Spanish the word for everywhere that is not a town: \emph{vivo en el campo} means you live out there, among the fields, whether or not you farm.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The ground itself, before anything is put on it.

\emph{El pueblo} is where people are; \emph{el campo} is what surrounds it. Between them you can already say roughly where somebody is from, which is most of what that question ever wants.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el campo}
  \item \emph{el pueblo}, then \emph{el campo}
  \item \emph{soy del campo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{campus} mean? (Flat open ground.) What was a \emph{campio}? (The man who fought on it — a champion.) And what does \emph{el campo} mean besides a field? (The countryside.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la granja]{la granja — a building named after what is in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C299-granja}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what does \emph{ni hablar} refuse? (The conversation.) And what did \emph{campus} mean? (Flat open ground.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el trigo — what this building was built to hold.
  \item el campo — the ground it stands on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{GRAN-ja}, stress on the first part. The \emph{g} is hard, and the \emph{j} is the scrape. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la granja} — \textquotedblleft{}the farm.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is Latin \textbf{granum}, the grain — the same grain you met being rubbed out of its husk in \emph{el trigo}. A \emph{granja} began as the building where that grain was kept, and then the name spread outwards over the yard, the animals and the whole holding.

English has the identical building twice. A \textbf{granary} is where the grain goes. A \textbf{grange} is the farmhouse that grew up around one, which is why so many English villages have a Grange in them and nobody remembers why.

This is a common way for names to work. The store gives its name to the farm, the way \emph{la sopa} took its name from the bread rather than the broth. The thing you kept was more worth naming than the place you kept it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The ground and now the buildings on it.

You have had \emph{el trigo} for a while as something that grows. \emph{La granja} is where it stops being a crop and starts being a store, and \emph{el campo} is the flat land both of them sit on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la granja}
  \item \emph{el campo}, then \emph{la granja}
  \item \emph{el trigo de la granja}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{granum}? (The grain.) What was a \emph{granja} before it was a farm? (The place the grain was stored.) And which English farmhouse is the same word? (A grange.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el ganado]{el ganado — the animals as a bank account}

\label{lesson:ES-C299-ganado}



\begin{quote}
What did \emph{campus} mean? (Flat open ground.) And what was a \emph{granja} before it was a farm? (Where the grain was stored.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la vaca — one of these, counted singly.
  \item el dinero — what this word is really about.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ga-NA-do}, stress in the middle. The \emph{g} is hard and the \emph{d} between vowels is soft, almost a \emph{th}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el ganado} — \textquotedblleft{}the livestock,\textquotedblright{} the animals of a farm taken together.

It is built on \emph{ganar}, to gain or to win, and it means, quite plainly, \textquotedblleft{}what has been gained.\textquotedblright{} Not the beasts as creatures. The beasts as the thing you have got.

English did exactly the same and hid it better. \textbf{Cattle} and \textbf{chattel} are one word split in two, both from Latin \emph{capitalis}, \textquotedblleft{}of the head\textquotedblright{} — property counted by the head. And \emph{capitalis} also gave \textbf{capital}, the money sense. So in English, as in Spanish, the herd and the fortune are the same idea.

That is why \emph{el ganado} covers cows and sheep and pigs without distinction. It is not a word about animals at all. It is a word about wealth that happens to walk around.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ground, buildings, and now the animals — and the animals turn out to be an account.

\emph{La vaca} is one cow. \emph{El ganado} is the whole herd seen from the ledger, which is how a farmer in any century has actually seen it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ganado}
  \item \emph{la granja}, then \emph{el ganado}
  \item \emph{el ganado del campo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ganar} mean? (To gain, to win.) So what is \emph{el ganado} literally? (What has been gained.) And which English word for money comes from counting animals by the head? (\emph{Capital}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cosecha]{la cosecha — a root you have met before}

\label{lesson:ES-C299-cosecha}



\begin{quote}
Three questions. What did \emph{campus} mean? (Flat open ground.) What is \emph{granum}? (Grain.) And what is \emph{el ganado}, literally? (What has been gained.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tomar — where you first took \emph{colligere} apart.
  \item la semilla — where this ends up starting again.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-SE-cha}, stress in the middle. The \emph{ch} is one sound, as in English \emph{church}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cosecha} — \textquotedblleft{}the harvest,\textquotedblright{} both the gathering and the crop gathered.

You have already done the hard part of this one. When \emph{tomar} was taken apart, the word Latin actually left behind turned out to be \emph{coger}, from \textbf{colligere} — \emph{com-}, together, and \emph{legere}, to pick. That is where \textbf{collect} comes from, and \textbf{coil}, and the \emph{leer} you read with.

\emph{Cosecha} is the same word wearing its finished-and-done form: \textbf{collecta}, \textquotedblleft{}the gathered-in.\textquotedblright{} So the harvest is not named for cutting or for work. It is named for the picking-up afterwards, which is the part that counts.

One use worth knowing. On a wine label, \emph{una buena cosecha} is a good vintage — English does the same thing, since a \textbf{vintage} is only a harvest with a year attached to it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of the farm, and one of them cost you almost nothing.

\emph{Colligere} was already in your hands. All that was new here was which shape it takes when the picking is over, and now the same root is doing work in three places at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cosecha}
  \item \emph{la granja} and \emph{la cosecha}, one after the other
  \item all four — \emph{el campo}, \emph{la granja}, \emph{el ganado}, \emph{la cosecha}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two pieces are in \emph{colligere}? (\emph{Com-}, together, and \emph{legere}, to pick.) Which English word is it most plainly? (\emph{Collect}.) And what does \emph{una buena cosecha} mean on a bottle? (A good vintage.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pastor]{el pastor — the one who feeds}

\label{lesson:ES-C299-pastor}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what did \emph{campus} mean? (Flat open ground.) What is \emph{el ganado} literally? (What has been gained.) And which two pieces are in \emph{colligere}? (\emph{Com-} and \emph{legere}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la oveja — what this person walks behind.
  \item el maestro — another person named for what they do.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pas-TOR}, stress on the end, and no accent needed because a word ending in \emph{-r} is expected there. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pastor} — \textquotedblleft{}the shepherd.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pascere} meant to put animals out to feed, and \emph{pastor} was the one who did it. Note what is not in the word: nothing about sheep, nothing about walking, nothing about a crook. Only the feeding.

That single idea fans out a long way in English. A \textbf{pasture} is the ground the animals are fed on. A \textbf{repast} is a meal — a feeding, taken again. And a \textbf{pastor} in a church is a shepherd of people, a metaphor so old it has stopped sounding like one.

The ending is the \emph{-or} you met on \emph{el tenedor}: the one who does the thing. So \emph{pastor} parses as neatly as \emph{tenedor} did, once you know that the thing being done is feeding.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el campo}, \emph{la granja}, \emph{el ganado}, \emph{la cosecha}, \emph{el pastor}.

Read in order they are a whole holding: the ground, the buildings, the animals, what comes off the land, and the person who keeps it moving. Say \emph{soy del campo} and every one of them is behind the sentence.

And three of the five were named for something other than themselves — a farm for its grain, a herd for its value, a harvest for the gathering. Spanish names things by what they are for. Once you expect that, half the words explain themselves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pastor}
  \item \emph{el pastor y la oveja}
  \item all five — \emph{el campo}, \emph{la granja}, \emph{el ganado}, \emph{la cosecha}, \emph{el pastor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{pascere} mean? (To put out to feed.) What is a \emph{repast}, at root? (A feeding again — a meal.) And why is a churchman called a pastor? (He is a shepherd of people.)
\end{tcolorbox}
